title: Government Agents: AI Agents Meet Tough Regulations — Mark Myshatyn, Los Alamos National Lab
talk_summary: The actionable content is mostly compliance-oriented: build for explainability, isolation, governance (SBOM, patching), and deployment portability to constrained environments.

takeaways.technique: Build for isolation and least-common-denominator deployment
takeaways.what_they_do: They require agent tools to run in isolated, self-hosted environments and recommend designing against the most restricted deployment target (DoD IL5) so the same artifact deploys anywhere.
takeaways.evidence_quote: if you can build in a DoD impact level 5 environment with that limited number of services from your cloud vendor, you can deploy anywhere

takeaways.technique: Software bill of materials and patching plan as a first-class artifact
takeaways.what_they_do: Procurement requires an SBOM and explicit open-source dependency and patching plans; they advise generating these proactively rather than reconstructing from build scripts.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we need a software bill of materials as we're doing this procurement with you

takeaways.technique: Explainability as an architectural requirement (decision provenance)
takeaways.what_they_do: They require agents to record how a decision was reached so outcomes can be trusted and defended after the fact, analogous to trusting staff.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we want to see that you've built for explanability ... how did you get to that decision?

takeaways.technique: Agent executes real code on real compute, not just chat output
takeaways.what_they_do: Their fusion-capsule agent reads papers, forms a hypothesis, then runs the generated code on HPC simulation assets rather than returning text.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we're actually executing that code on our high performance computing assets
